opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really important piece, and it's something I've come to appreciate more over time. There's a lot you can do before release: internal red-teaming, structured evaluations for dangerous capabilities, external testers poking at the model, all the policy and frontier safety work. That pre-release work is essential and it's never something we'd skip. But no matter how thorough you are, a relatively small group of people trying to anticipate every way a model will be used is never going to cover the full space of what happens when millions of people get their hands on it.

So part of the value of an experimental release is that it's explicitly framed as "this is early, we want to learn from it." You get a much richer signal about where the model is genuinely helpful, where it's falling short, and where there are behaviors you didn't anticipate. Some of that is about safety in the narrow sense, but a lot of it is subtler things. Is the model overly cautious in places where it really shouldn't be? Is it confidently wrong in a particular domain? Does it behave strangely over very long conversations or in agentic settings that weren't well represented in your evals? Those are things you often only discover at scale.

The way I think about it is that it's a layered approach. You do the rigorous pre-release testing so you're confident there aren't serious risks before anything goes out. Then the experimental phase is a way to gather feedback in a more controlled setting, with clear labeling and the ability to iterate quickly, before something becomes a stable, widely deployed product that people build on. That feedback loop goes straight back into training and evaluation. If people find failure modes, those become new evals and new training data, and the next version is better for it.

I'd also say it keeps you honest. It's very easy to optimize for benchmarks and internal metrics and convince yourself the model is great. Real usage is the ultimate ground truth. So I see real-world feedback not as a replacement for safety testing, but as a necessary complement to it, the part that tells you what your tests were missing.

r001.rationale: The response describes experimental releases as a way to gather real-world feedback about unexpected behaviors and says this feedback is a necessary complement to pre-release safety testing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think real-world feedback is one of the most important and, honestly, one of the most underappreciated parts of safety testing. There's a limit to what you can learn in the lab. You can build evals, you can red-team internally, you can bring in external groups to probe the model, and all of that is valuable. But those efforts are fundamentally bounded by the imagination of the people designing them. The space of things people actually do with a model is vastly larger than the space of things you can anticipate ahead of time.

So the way I think about it is in stages. Before anything goes out, you want to be confident that the model clears a bar on the things you can measure: the known categories of harm, the known failure modes, the capability thresholds that matter. That's the pre-deployment gate, and you shouldn't skip it. But once you pass that gate, an experimental release is really a way of expanding your test set to include the world. You're getting signal on behaviours that nobody on the team thought to check, interaction patterns that only emerge at scale, the ways people route around your intended use cases.

The key is that the release has to be structured so that the feedback loop is actually tight. That means a limited rollout, good instrumentation, clear channels for people to report problems, and a real willingness to pull back or change course if something comes up. If you release experimentally but you've already committed to the launch regardless of what you learn, then you're not really doing safety testing, you're just doing marketing with extra steps. The honesty of the process depends on the feedback being able to change the outcome.

I'd also say the feedback is useful in both directions. Sometimes you learn the model has a problem you missed. But just as often you learn that something you were worried about doesn't actually show up in practice, or shows up far less than you'd feared, and that lets you calibrate. Over time, that calibration is what makes your pre-deployment testing better. The lab evals and the real-world signal should be feeding each other, so that each release cycle, your ability to predict what will happen before launch gets a little closer to what actually does.

r001.rationale: The response describes an experimental release as a way to gather real-world feedback and expand safety testing to behaviors and interactions that pre-release evaluations may miss.

astra-6.text:
I think real-world feedback is an important part of safety testing, because there’s a limit to what you can learn in a controlled setting. You can do extensive evaluations and red teaming, but people will find ways of interacting with a model that you didn’t anticipate, and some failures only become apparent in the context of an actual use case.

That doesn’t mean you release something broadly just to find out whether it’s safe. It argues for staged releases, where the exposure is limited and you have ways to monitor problems, investigate reports, and roll back if necessary. The feedback should then feed into better evaluations and changes to the model or the surrounding system.

And you have to be careful about what you conclude: not receiving reports of harm isn’t the same as demonstrating safety. Real-world feedback is another source of evidence, alongside the testing you do before release.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world feedback is an important part of safety testing and describes gathering it through staged, limited model releases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think real-world feedback is an important complement to the testing you can do before release. In a controlled evaluation, you’re inevitably making assumptions about how people will use the model. Once people actually interact with it, you discover use cases and failure modes that you hadn’t anticipated.

But that shouldn’t mean releasing something broadly and hoping to learn whether it’s safe. You want a staged process: do the upfront testing, start with a limited release, monitor what happens, and have the ability to respond quickly or pull back. The feedback should then feed into both improving the model and improving your evaluations, so that a failure you discover in the world becomes something you can test for before the next release.

And the absence of reported problems isn’t itself strong evidence of safety. Some problems are difficult to observe or only emerge over time. So I’d see real-world feedback as one part of an ongoing safety process, rather than a final stamp of approval.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback from people interacting with a limited experimental release complements pre-release testing and contributes to ongoing safety testing.
